idiom_name: ExecutionContext + Future as the performer pool, or Akka/Pekko MessageDispatcher bound to actor mailboxes
implementation_notes: scala.concurrent supplies the performer pool: Future { ... } submits a message to the implicit ExecutionContext - ExecutionContext.global is a ForkJoinPool sized to available processors, and ExecutionContext.fromExecutor(new ThreadPoolExecutor(...)) wraps a bounded, named pool when the work blocks. Akka/Pekko goes further and names the pattern literally: a MessageDispatcher binds a set of actors (the performers) to an executor and owns their mailboxes, with Dispatcher vs PinnedDispatcher, a configurable thread-pool or fork-join executor, and throughput controlling how many messages an actor drains before the thread moves on. The classic hand-written dispatcher loop is only worth it for bespoke selection policies; otherwise let Future/actor scheduling carry it.
pitfalls: ExecutionContext.global is a ForkJoinPool: blocking calls starve the pool and can make it grow to thousands of threads; use blocking { } for short blocks and a dedicated executor for long ones.
An implicit ExecutionContext leaks between components: a hard-coded global in a library makes the caller's pool unconfigurable and hides where the work runs.
Futures complete in nondeterministic order, so a dispatcher built on them loses message ordering unless ordering is restored (per-key queues, single-threaded pools, or an actor per key).
Actors must not block on the default dispatcher (Akka's own documentation marks it as incorrect code): blocking actors need DispatcherSelector.blocking() or a separate pool.

The default dispatcher's throughput setting batches messages per actor; raising it improves throughput but delays other actors, which is exactly the fairness/serialization trade-off of a central dispatcher.
